transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-18 16:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Sofia Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO, Quorra), Liam O'Neal (Lead Eng), Priya Rao (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy): Quick host API + console orientation for Quorra Labs focused on chat and text generation basics — streaming behavior, key tunables (temperature, max_tokens), retry and backoff patterns, and costs/latency tradeoffs. Discussed options for hosted vs dedicated vs private; security & compliance checklist requested; agreed on a short POC for latency baseline.

Topics: streaming responses, idempotency, request retries/backoff, temperature and top_p guidance, batching and KV cache mention, console Optimize tips, security (SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS), routing and fallback, sandbox keys and benchmarking plan.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jared: hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is Jared from Redwood, i'm the AE, with sofia our se. how's everyone doing? 
[00:10] Maya: good, thanks; excited to see the hosted setup; we wanted a quick practical runthrough not just slides. 
[00:18] Liam: yes want to understand streaming and retries — our app is real-time-ish so latency matters. 
[00:25] Jared: perfect, we'll show the api, a console tour and then a few optimize tips for cost. sofia will demo the sandbox live. 
[00:32] Sofia: quick note, i might stumble audio wise — the demo uses a sandbox key; i'll show how streaming chunks arrive and where retries happen. 
[00:40] Priya: great. we also need to surface who owns security signoffs — SOC two docs and SSO are big for us. 
[00:47] Jared: totally, we'll cover that near the end. okay sofia over to you. 

[01:10] Sofia: (shares screen) starting with a basic chat request — the payload includes messages, model, and params: temperature, max_tokens, top_p, and a client_id for idempotency. on streaming you'll get chunks as they generate, and we provide a final chunk with finish_reason. 
[01:36] Sofia: note — streaming can be tuned: reduce chunk granularity to reduce network chattiness, or increase it if you want more immediate partial tokens. also we do automatic prefix caching for repeated system prompts — saves tokens. 
[01:54] Liam: is that the KV cache? sometimes docs call it K-V cash and we were confused. 
[02:00] Sofia: yes it's the KV cache, sorry transcription on some docs says 'K-V cash' hehe. the cache stores prefix key/value so repeat context doesn't cost full recompute. 

[02:20] Maya: how do retries look in practice? we have flaky mobile networks so intermittent failures matter. 
[02:26] Sofia: good question. we recommend an idempotency key per user-turn, then client retries with exponential backoff (base 200-500ms jitter). server-side we have automatic request de-dup when idempotency key matches within a window. 
[02:46] Sofia: also the console shows a per-request timeline — you can see where a retry occurred and why. 

[03:10] Liam: what about partial responses — if we re-try do we replay partial streamed tokens? 
[03:16] Sofia: you should design streams to be resumable; for us we recommend buffering complete chunks on client and resend only missing ranges when possible. short answer: you will likely restart generation but with idempotency and small prompt prefix the visible duplicate is small. 

[03:40] Jared: let's talk params quickly — temperature controls randomness, 0.0 is deterministic, 0.7 typical for creative, top_p can be used instead or together. we also expose max_new_tokens and max_total_tokens to keep costs bounded. 
[04:02] Priya: any rule of thumb for cost vs quality? 
[04:08] Sofia: start with lower token budgets and tune temperature; lots of customers find setting system prompt concise and caching system instructions reduces token use. also batching similar requests (if you can tolerate a few ms) improves throughput and unit cost. 

[04:35] Maya: dedicated vs hosted — we care about predictable latency and data isolation. where does hosted fall short? 
[04:43] Jared: hosted gives fastest time-to-value and managed infra, but if you need strict network isolation or on-prem KMS, Redwood Private is the option. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools — predictable throughput and isolation without a full private control plane. 
[05:05] Maya: ok and SLAs? 
[05:08] Jared: we have SLA tiers for Dedicated and Private; hosted has standard uptime and strong regional redundancy — we can include specifics in the security pack. 

[05:30] Liam: about latency numbers — can you give ballpark p95 for a 2k token response? 
[05:36] Sofia: depends on model and quantization; for a 2k token stream on our fast path you'll often see 600-900ms to first token on an optimized model in the hosted pool, tail depends on total tokens. for strict low p95 you may want Dedicated with pinned instance types. these are rough—benchmarking is required. 
[05:58] Liam: that's fair. we'd like to run a 48-hour latency POC. 
[06:02] Jared: great, we can arrange that — sofia will send the test plan. 

[06:20] Priya: what's Optimize in the console — i've seen mentions of recommendations. 
[06:25] Sofia: Optimize is a set of suggestions: batching profiles, caching candidates, quantization choices per model, and cost projection per route. it surfaces unusual token usage and suggests lower-cost model variants. you can pin rollouts and auto-fallback policies. 
[06:46] Maya: can Optimize recommend quantization safely? we are worried about quality regressions. 
[06:50] Sofia: yes it flags potential quality regressions tied to a prompt set and you can run A/B rollouts with evals. it's tied to the eval harness. we won't recommend blind quant — we'll show model delta metrics. 

[07:12] Liam: security again: SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS integration — can you support customer-managed keys? 
[07:19] Jared: Private supports customer KMS via our control plane; Dedicated can be configured with strict logging and tenancy controls. Hosted encrypts at rest and integrates with KMS for transit keys — we'll include specifics. 

[07:40] Priya: any red flags for procurement? certs? 
[07:43] Jared: SOC2 Type II available, ISO in progress, we have data processing addendum templates. legal/procurement often ask about data residency and retention — we support region pinning and configurable retention. 

[08:05] Maya: what about fallbacks — if a model fails do you have automatic routing to smaller models? 
[08:11] Sofia: yes, smart routing can fallback to a compatible variant; you can define policy by latency or cost thresholds. e.g., if the primary model misses an SLO, route to a lower-cost variant. 

[08:30] Liam: curious about developer ergonomics — SDKs, trace ids, and observability. 
[08:35] Jared: SDKs in major langs, trace id per request, console shows token-level breakdown and per-route latency. we also expose tracing hooks for your APM. 

[08:50] Priya: for the POC who should do what? 
[08:53] Jared: action items — we'll send pricing and security docs; sofia will build test plan; you send target traffic and SLOs. 

[09:05] Maya: timeline — product wants a recommendation in 2 weeks. 
[09:09] Jared: ok that aligns — we'll aim to have materials and a POC kickoff by next week. 

[09:20] (cross talk) 
[09:25] Sofia: small demo note — when using streaming, watch client-side backpressure; if you drop sockets retries will trigger — implement reconnect and resume logic where possible. 

[09:44] Liam: thanks this is helpful; can you also share a short script to reproduce p95 numbers? 
[09:49] Sofia: yes we'll include a simple load script and a config for the sandbox. 

[10:02] Jared: recap: send pricing, security pack, sandbox key + console guide, runbook for latency POC, schedule private networking deep-dive. next call: POC kickoff (target Aug 24).
[10:20] Maya: thanks all. 
[10:23] Meeting ends — ~48 minutes

Notes on transcript quality: some system words mis-transcribed (SAML -> 'sam-el', KV cache -> 'K-V cash'), occasional speaker mislabels, and filler words preserved.
